title: Porcupines: Little Stabby Cutie Pies
summary: Josh and Chuck explore porcupines: the Old World (Europe, Africa, Asia) versus New World (North, South, Central America) groups, how their quills differ (length, barbs, quills mixed with fur), defensive behaviors like rattling, puffing up, and backward charges, and the myth that they shoot quills. They cover diet and nuisance behavior (sodium cravings, plywood glue, road salt, girdling trees), nocturnal habits, swimming, ecosystem role in seed dispersal, lifespan, mating (urine spraying, barbed tail), gestation and porcupet young, the danger of quills to dogs and why to go straight to a vet, myths about clipping quills, and porcupine escapees in the UK. The episode closes with a listener mail from Don the Black Cowboy about Black cowboys and ferriers.

segments.title: Opening banter and porcupine overview
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about cute porcupines, Teddy Bear the porcupine videos, and the Old World versus New World division of porcupines, noting that all porcupines have quills used for defense.

segments.title: Differences between Old World and New World porcupines
segments.summary: Old World porcupines are mostly terrestrial with longer quills up to about twenty inches that can have black and white bands; New World porcupines climb trees, have shorter quills, and have barbed quills mixed with fur. Defensive tactics include puffing up, rattling, charging backward, and crested porcupines.
topics: Old World vs New World porcupines

segments.title: Porcupine quills, myths, and tire punctures
segments.summary: Quills are modified keratin hair. The hosts debunk the myth that porcupines shoot quills, note that loose quills can puncture tires, and discuss hunting threats including lions, owls, pythons, and fishers.

segments.title: Porcupine diet, salt cravings, and tree girdling
segments.summary: Porcupines are generalist herbivores that eat plants, bark, and crops, and seek sodium from sweaty tool handles, plywood glue, road salt residue, and car parts. In winter they specialize on inner bark, which can girdle and kill trees; wire wrapping is a suggested deterrent.

segments.title: Porcupine behavior, lifespan, swimming, and ecosystem role
segments.summary: Porcupines are nocturnal and mostly solitary, do not hibernate, and New World species swim to gather aquatic plants. They reuse abandoned dens and disturb soil, which helps seed dispersal. Lifespans in the wild range from about three to ten years, with captive animals living longer.

segments.title: Porcupine mating, gestation, and porcupets
segments.summary: Males compete and spray urine on the female during courtship; the barbed tail is kept to the side during mating. Gestation runs about 112 to 217 days, litters are usually one to four, and young stay with mothers for months, with quills hardening days after birth.
